newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ rates shoot higher at close as comments hit TWI.
newsitem.headline: NZ rates shoot higher at close as comments hit TWI.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 92.94 (PREV 92.95) 90-DAYS 7.35 (PREV 7.30)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.60 PCT (PREV 7.65) US 5-YR 6.16 (PREV 6.15)
RBNZ MCI NZ/MCI 763.87 (PREV 780.78) Reuters NZ MCI -61 vs -44

New Zealand 90-day bank bill rates shot to 7.35 percent at Wednesday's close as the currency's Trade-Weighted Index dropped to its lowest level since October 1996 on the back of comments by Treasurer Winston Peters.
The TWI dipped to an intra-day low of 65.97 from 66.31 at Tuesday's close, but came back to finish at around 66.02.
The last time it was down round those levels was on October 11, when its low was 65.93.

Peters told a business lunch in Sydney he saw further weakness in the currency, which has fallen five percent since February. Foreign exchange dealers said the kiwi had looked vulnerable and the market was looking for an excuse to sell it when Peters' comments were released.

At 7.35 percent 90-day bills were five basis points above their Tuesday closing levels, taking the Monetary Conditions Index to 763.87, 61 basis points below the Reserve Bank's desired level. The bank has said it would tolerate conditions 50 basis points either side of its assumptions.
One money market dealer said traders were reluctant to throw themselves into selling short-dated assets, because the low inflation environment favoured interest rate products.

He noted that most assets other than the short-dated bank bills were reasonably well bid, as the market sold instruments that were coming under the scrutiny of the RBNZ, and remained happy to hold everything else.
But as much as the money market market wanted to be bullish, traders were spooked by the possibility of further weakness in the kiwi.
The currency is seen retaining its heavy tone ahead of balance of payments data due on Friday, which is expected to show a widening in the current account deficit.
Economists polled by Reuters on average expect a deficit in the year to March of NZ$4.111 billion, from $3.913 billion in the December year.
Dealers said the overnight cash rate, doggedly holding up at 7.6 percent, was also making it expensive to hold the physical bills.

Meanwhile, the 11/06 bond finished the day one pip stronger at 6.87 percent, and bond dealers said they were surprised it hadn't performed better ahead of Thursday's government bond tender and expected benign inflation data next week.
The tender, of NZ$150 million of 02/01 and 07/09 bonds, is expected to be well supported.
The mid bond ended flat at 6.71 percent.
